title: Development & Global Inequality
description: What development means, how we measure it, why the world is unequal, and the strategies used to close the gap.

notes.heading: 📌 What is Development?
notes.body: Development means improving people's quality of life — not just how much money a country has, but whether people are healthy, educated, safe and free to make choices. It has several dimensions: economic (income, jobs, industry), social (health, education, equality, access to clean water and sanitation), political (democracy, stability, rights) and environmental (clean air, sustainable resource use). A country can be rich in income but still underdeveloped in other ways — for example, if wealth is held by a small elite or if pollution makes people ill. Development is also uneven WITHIN countries: capital cities and coastal regions are often far more developed than remote rural areas. The global development gap is the difference in wealth and quality of life between the richest and poorest countries and people.

notes.heading: 📎 Classifying Countries
notes.body: Geographers group countries by their level of development. High-income countries (HICs) — such as the UK, Japan and Germany — have wealthy economies based mainly on services and advanced industry, high life expectancy and near-universal education. Low-income countries (LICs) — such as Afghanistan and several countries in sub-Saharan Africa — have low average incomes, economies dependent on farming and raw materials, and weaker services. Newly emerging economies (NEEs) or emerging markets — such as Brazil, India, China, Nigeria and Mexico — are industrialising rapidly, with fast-growing incomes but still significant poverty. Older labels like First World/Third World or a simple rich North vs poor South divide (the Brandt line) are now considered outdated: many southern countries have developed fast, and every country contains rich and poor people. Labels are useful for spotting patterns, but always remember they hide huge variety.

notes.heading: 🔑 Measuring Development
notes.body: Single economic measures are quick but limited. GDP per capita (gross domestic product divided by population) measures average income; GNI per capita is similar but includes income earned abroad. Both are averages — they hide inequality, so a country with a few billionaires can look rich on average while most people are poor. Social indicators reveal quality of life directly: life expectancy (average age a person can expect to live), literacy rate (percentage of adults who can read and write), infant mortality rate (deaths of babies under 1 year old per 1,000 live births) and access to clean water. Because no single measure tells the whole story, the United Nations created the Human Development Index (HDI) — a score between 0 and 1 combining income (GNI per capita), health (life expectancy) and education (years of schooling). Norway typically scores near 0.96, while the lowest-scoring countries score around 0.4. Even HDI leaves out inequality, freedom and the environment.

notes.heading: 🔑 Why is the World Unequal? Causes of the Development Gap
notes.body: Inequality has many interlocking causes. Historical: colonialism saw European powers extract resources and wealth from colonised countries, draw arbitrary borders and leave weak institutions at independence; the slave trade devastated African societies for centuries. Environmental: some countries face natural hazards (earthquakes, droughts, tropical diseases like malaria), poor soils or hostile climates; being landlocked (no coastline) makes trade expensive. Social: where girls are denied education or healthcare is poor, populations grow fast and productivity stays low; lack of clean water keeps children ill and out of school. Economic and political: poor countries often depend on exporting cheap raw materials (cocoa, copper) while importing expensive manufactured goods — an unfair trade balance; heavy debt repayments drain money from schools and hospitals; corruption and war destroy wealth and drive away investment. These factors reinforce each other in a cycle of poverty that is hard to escape.

notes.heading: 📎 Aid: Types and Effectiveness
notes.body: Aid is the transfer of money, goods, skills or expertise from richer to poorer countries. Types include: emergency (short-term) aid — food, water, tents and medical help after disasters such as earthquakes or famines; long-term (development) aid — projects like schools, wells and clinics that improve lives over years; bilateral aid — given directly from one country's government to another; multilateral aid — channelled through international organisations like the World Bank or UN agencies; and NGO/charity aid — delivered by organisations such as Oxfam or the Red Cross. Tied aid comes with strings attached — for example, the receiving country must spend it on goods from the donor country — which reduces its value. Aid can transform lives, but critics point out problems: corruption can divert funds, large projects can be inappropriate for local needs, and dependence on aid can discourage local enterprise. The most effective aid is usually small-scale, locally run and designed with the community it serves.

notes.heading: 🔑 Fair Trade and Trade Justice
notes.body: Trade is the biggest flow of money between rich and poor countries — far larger than aid — but the rules often favour the powerful. Poor countries typically export low-value raw materials (cocoa beans, coffee, cotton) whose world prices swing wildly, and import expensive manufactured goods. Farmers may receive only a tiny share of the final shop price. Fair Trade is a movement that guarantees producers a minimum price plus an extra premium for community projects, in return for decent working conditions and environmental standards. Shoppers recognise Fairtrade-certified chocolate, coffee, bananas and cotton. Benefits: farmers get stable, higher incomes and communities fund schools and clinics. Criticisms: the scheme reaches only a small share of farmers, certification costs money, and some argue it does not fix the underlying trade rules. Wider trade justice campaigns push for fairer global rules — for example, cutting the subsidies rich countries pay their own farmers, which undercut poor farmers.

notes.heading: 💡 Reducing the Gap: Strategies that Work
notes.body: No single strategy closes the development gap — countries that develop successfully combine several. Education is perhaps the most powerful: every extra year of schooling raises a person's future income, and educating girls lowers birth rates and improves child health. Microfinance — tiny loans to poor entrepreneurs, pioneered by the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh — lets people start small businesses without needing a bank account or collateral. Debt relief cancels unpayable debts so money can fund services instead. Appropriate (intermediate) technology — simple, cheap, locally maintainable solutions like hand pumps, solar lamps and fuel-efficient stoves — often helps more than expensive high-tech projects. Industrialisation and adding value to raw materials (processing cocoa into chocolate at home rather than exporting beans) keeps more wealth in the country. Good governance — stable, honest government — underpins everything. Top-down mega-projects (giant dams, motorways) can bring growth but may displace people and enrich elites; bottom-up community projects are slower but reach the poorest directly.

flashcards.definition: The improvement of people's quality of life — including income, health, education, equality and freedom — not just economic wealth.
flashcards.example: A country developing successfully might raise life expectancy and literacy as well as average income.

flashcards.definition: The total value of goods and services produced by a country in a year, divided by its population — a rough measure of average income.
flashcards.example: Switzerland's GDP per capita is many times higher than Malawi's, but both figures hide internal inequality.

flashcards.definition: A UN measure of development from 0 to 1 combining income, life expectancy and years of schooling.
flashcards.example: Norway scores around 0.96 on the HDI, while the lowest-scoring countries are near 0.4.

flashcards.definition: The percentage of adults in a country who can read and write — a key social indicator of development.
flashcards.example: HICs have literacy rates near 100%; in some LICs fewer than half of adults can read.

flashcards.definition: The average number of years a newborn can expect to live, reflecting healthcare, nutrition and sanitation.
flashcards.example: Life expectancy is over 80 years in Japan but under 60 in the poorest countries.

flashcards.definition: The number of babies who die before their first birthday per 1,000 live births — a sensitive indicator of poverty and healthcare.
flashcards.example: High infant mortality usually signals poor sanitation, malnutrition and limited access to clinics.

flashcards.definition: A country that is industrialising and getting richer rapidly but still has significant poverty — between LIC and HIC status.
flashcards.example: India, Brazil and Nigeria are classic NEEs with fast-growing industries alongside large poor populations.

flashcards.definition: A scheme guaranteeing producers in poor countries a minimum price plus a community premium, in return for decent labour and environmental standards.
flashcards.example: Fairtrade-certified cocoa farmers receive a stable price even when world market prices crash.

flashcards.definition: Aid given directly from the government of one country to the government of another.
flashcards.example: The UK funding school-building in a partner country is bilateral aid.

flashcards.definition: Aid funded by many countries together and distributed through international organisations.
flashcards.example: The World Bank and UN agencies deliver multilateral aid such as vaccination programmes.

flashcards.definition: Aid given with conditions attached — typically that the money must be spent on goods or services from the donor country.
flashcards.example: A loan for a railway that must be built using the donor's companies is tied aid, reducing its value to the recipient.

flashcards.definition: Very small loans given to poor entrepreneurs who cannot borrow from normal banks, letting them start or expand tiny businesses.
flashcards.example: The Grameen Bank in Bangladesh lends small sums, often to women, to buy a sewing machine or market stall.

questions.stem: What does development mean in geography?
choices: Building more factories
Improving people's quality of life, including wealth, health, education and freedom
Increasing a country's population
Exporting more raw materials
questions.explanation: Development is broader than economic growth — it means raising quality of life across health, education, equality and security, as well as income.

questions.stem: What does GDP per capita measure?
choices: The total population of a country
The value of goods and services produced per person in a year
The percentage of adults who can read
The number of babies who die each year
questions.explanation: GDP per capita is gross domestic product divided by population — a rough guide to average income. It says nothing directly about health or education.

questions.stem: Why can GDP per capita be misleading as a measure of development?
choices: It is only calculated every ten years
It is an average that hides inequality — a few very rich people can make a mostly poor country look wealthy
It cannot be measured in poor countries
It includes health and education data
questions.explanation: Averages conceal distribution. If a small elite holds most of the wealth, GDP per capita looks healthy while the majority remain in poverty — which is why social indicators are needed too.

questions.stem: Which three components make up the Human Development Index (HDI)?
choices: Income, military strength and land area
Income (GNI per capita), health (life expectancy) and education (years of schooling)
Rainfall, temperature and population
Exports, imports and debt
questions.explanation: HDI combines an economic measure (GNI per capita), a health measure (life expectancy) and an education measure (schooling) into a single 0-1 score, giving a broader picture than income alone.

questions.stem: A newly emerging economy (NEE) is best described as a country that:
choices: Is the poorest in the world
Has been wealthy for centuries
Is industrialising and getting richer rapidly, but still has significant poverty
Has no industry at all
questions.explanation: NEEs such as India, Brazil and Nigeria sit between LICs and HICs: their industries and incomes are growing fast, but poverty and inequality remain widespread.

questions.stem: How did colonialism contribute to today's development gap?
choices: It spread wealth evenly around the world
European powers extracted resources and wealth, and left colonised countries with weak institutions and arbitrary borders
It built modern industries in every colony
It had no lasting economic effects
questions.explanation: Colonial economies were organised to export raw materials to the coloniser, not to develop locally. At independence many countries were left with weak institutions, poor infrastructure and borders that fuelled conflict.

questions.stem: Why is being landlocked (having no coastline) a disadvantage for development?
choices: Landlocked countries cannot grow crops
Trade becomes expensive because goods must cross neighbouring countries to reach a seaport
The climate is always worse inland
Landlocked countries have no rivers
questions.explanation: Most world trade moves by sea. Landlocked countries depend on transit through neighbours — paying fees, tariffs and transport costs — which makes their exports less competitive.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes the unfair trade balance faced by many LICs?
choices: They export expensive manufactured goods and import cheap raw materials
They export cheap raw materials with unstable prices and import expensive manufactured goods
They trade equally with all countries
They refuse to trade internationally
questions.explanation: LICs typically sell low-value commodities like cocoa or copper, whose prices swing wildly, while buying costly manufactured products. Processing raw materials at home would keep far more value in the country.

questions.stem: What does Fair Trade guarantee to producers in poorer countries?
choices: Free machinery from donor governments
A minimum price for their goods plus a premium for community projects
That no other countries can sell the same crop
Automatic membership of the United Nations
questions.explanation: Fair Trade certification guarantees farmers a floor price even when world prices collapse, plus an extra premium invested in community projects such as schools and clinics — in return for decent labour and environmental standards.

choices: Aid that is never delivered
Aid given with conditions, usually that the money must be spent on goods or services from the donor country
Aid shared between many donor countries
Aid given only after natural disasters
questions.explanation: Tied aid comes with strings attached — typically the recipient must buy from the donor's companies. This inflates costs and channels much of the money back to the donor, reducing the real benefit.

questions.stem: After an earthquake destroys a town, food, tents and emergency medical teams are flown in. What type of aid is this?
choices: Long-term development aid
Multilateral aid
Emergency (short-term) aid
Tied aid
questions.explanation: Emergency aid provides immediate relief — food, water, shelter and medicine — in the days after a disaster. Rebuilding schools and infrastructure afterwards would be long-term development aid.

questions.stem: Why do critics argue that large amounts of foreign aid can sometimes fail to reduce poverty?
choices: Aid always makes things worse
Corruption can divert funds, big projects may not fit local needs, and dependence can discourage local enterprise
Poor countries do not need schools or wells
Aid is always spent on weapons
questions.explanation: Aid works best when it is small-scale, locally managed and designed with communities. Aid can fail when corrupt officials siphon it off, when inappropriate mega-projects collapse without maintenance, or when long-term dependence undermines local business.

questions.stem: Why is educating girls often called one of the most powerful development strategies?
choices: Educated girls pay more tax immediately
Educated women earn more, marry later, have fewer and healthier children, and are more likely to educate their own children — breaking the cycle of poverty
Schools for girls are cheaper to build
It only benefits the girls themselves
questions.explanation: Girls' education has multiplier effects: higher income, lower birth rates, better child health and nutrition, and children who are themselves more likely to attend school — benefits that ripple across generations.

questions.stem: A village without electricity is given simple solar lamps that local people can repair, rather than a connection to a distant coal power station. What development approach does this represent?
choices: Top-down mega-project
Tied aid
Appropriate (intermediate) technology
Free trade
questions.explanation: Appropriate technology is cheap, simple, suited to local conditions and locally maintainable — like solar lamps, hand pumps and fuel-efficient stoves. It often helps the poorest more than expensive high-tech schemes they cannot maintain.

questions.stem: Country X exports raw cocoa beans and imports finished chocolate. Country Y processes its cocoa into chocolate at home and exports that instead. Which country keeps more wealth, and why?
choices: Country X — raw materials always sell for the highest prices
Country Y — processing adds value, so far more of the final price stays in the country
Both keep the same amount
Country X — because transport costs are lower
questions.explanation: Most of the value in a chocolate bar comes from processing and branding, not the raw beans. Countries that add value to their raw materials capture more income, create skilled jobs and reduce dependence on unstable commodity prices.
